name: plugin
intent: Let a host application acquire behaviour from independently deployed modules that it discovers and links at configuration or start-up time, so new features, backends or device support can be added without recompiling or redeploying the host.
problem: The behaviours a system must offer vary by deployment (customer, environment, backend, hardware) or grow after the host has shipped; hard-wiring every implementation behind a factory method or a configuration switch means each new variant edits core code and forces a rebuild and redeploy of the whole application.
context: Systems whose capability set is not fully known at build time: third-party or per-customer extensions, drivers and storage backends, editor and build tooling, test runners, media pipelines. It applies wherever a stable extension point can be published, the contract can be versioned, and the runtime can bind code after compilation (shared libraries, class or module loading, plugin packages).
benefits: Open for extension, closed for modification: a new capability is a new plugin plus a descriptor entry, and the host core is not edited.
Independent release cycles: plugins are built, versioned and deployed separately, so one host build serves many deployment compositions.
One explicit place for configuration: discovery and binding happen in a registry or descriptor instead of conditional logic scattered across factories.
Ecosystem leverage: third parties can extend the system against a published contract, and optional or experimental features can be shipped or dropped without touching the host build.
Isolation of volatile code: unstable per-deployment behaviour sits behind the extension point, which keeps the core small and lets a contract-level compliance suite stand in for testing every plugin.

Late binding matches operations: the same artifact runs in development, test and production with different plugin sets, and capabilities can be enabled or removed by configuration and deploy rather than by release.
tradeoffs: The extension point becomes a public product: once plugins exist outside the team, every contract change must stay compatible with code the core team does not own, so versioning, deprecation windows and a shared compliance suite become permanent core-team work, and a breaking change strands the ecosystem.

Plugins execute with the host's privileges unless isolated; one compromised or careless extension is a supply-chain incident, and the isolation that contains it (separate class loaders or contexts, subprocesses, sandboxes) adds latency, serialization and deployment weight.

Failures move from compile time to load or run time: toolchain, ABI and version mismatches show up as a plugin that will not load or crashes in production (Go demands an identical toolchain and identical dependency sources, Rust has no stable ABI, .NET silently loads a duplicate contract assembly), and some runtimes cannot unload a plugin at all.

Lifecycle machinery is easy to get subtly wrong: registration order and activation timing change visible behaviour, and unloading leaks memory, handles or threads back into the host, so hot reload is expensive or unsupported.

Two plugins can depend on conflicting versions of the same library (or of the host contract) and the host has to own a resolution policy; without isolation contexts or pinned dependencies, whichever copy loads first silently wins.

Every invocation crosses at least one indirection (registry lookup, dynamic dispatch, sometimes a process boundary), and one slow synchronous plugin stalls the host's pipeline while the strongest isolation levels cost the most latency.

participants.responsibility: The stable application that defines the extension points, owns discovery and the plugin lifecycle, and invokes plugin behaviour at the published seams without knowing concrete plugin types.
The interface or function table a plugin must implement, plus its documented semantics; the contract is the only compile-time dependency the host and the plugin share.
The services, domain objects and callbacks the host publishes to plugins; everything else about the host stays hidden behind this interface.

An independently built and deployed module that implements the contract (usually offering a factory for its implementation), and declares its identity, version and target contract version in a descriptor.
Discovers available plugins from descriptors or runtime metadata, validates them against the contract version, holds the id-to-plugin map, and orders activation and deactivation.
Constructs the implementation for a plugin kind, hiding how the object is obtained (reflection, a name lookup, a constructor inside the loaded module) from the host.
Keeps plugin code apart from the host and from other plugins - class loader, load context, subprocess or sandbox; optional for code you own, mandatory once plugins are not fully trusted.

use_cases: IDEs, editors and build tools whose feature set grows through extensions (Eclipse, VS Code, webpack, ESLint, pytest, RuboCop).
Servers and frameworks that pick a codec, transport, storage or auth backend per deployment (JDBC drivers via ServiceLoader, .NET plugin hosts, Kafka connectors).
Infrastructure tooling that hosts independently released providers, such as Terraform providers over gRPC or Vault secret engines.
Media, imaging and device software that adds codecs, effects or drivers after the main program ships (Apache httpd modules, GStreamer, DAW and imaging plugins).
Document and data pipelines where per-customer transformation or validation steps are shipped as separate packages (Python entry points, Ruby gems).
Applications that must support tenant- or customer-specific behaviour without a private build per customer, composed at start-up from a plugin directory or a configuration list.
AI agent systems where tools, memory backends and LLMs are loaded as plugins (LangChain agents, semantic kernel plugins).
Cloud-native platforms that must support tenant-specific backends or third-party integrations without redeploying the control plane (Kubernetes operators, service mesh extensions).
DevOps and CI/CD pipelines where steps, reporters or cloud integrations are added as plugins (Jenkins plugins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI job templates).
Observability platforms where collectors, processors and exporters are pluginable (OpenTelemetry collectors, Grafana datasources and panels).
Editor ecosystems that declare contributions in manifests and run extension code behind a host boundary, as in Visual Studio Code's Extension Host and contribution points.
Infrastructure CLIs that launch provider binaries over a versioned RPC contract and negotiate compatibility, as in Terraform's Plugin Protocol and provider servers.
Web servers assembled from independently built dynamic modules loaded at startup or restart, as in Apache HTTP Server's DSO and mod_so module system.
avoid_when: The implementation set is small, fixed and owned by you: a Strategy, an abstract factory or plain dependency injection is simpler and stays compile-time checked.
Host and implementations are always built and shipped together: linking them statically and calling a registration function avoids the public-contract burden.
Behaviour must switch per request rather than be composed per deployment: a Feature Toggle or a Strategy selected from configuration is the right knob.
The capability set is known and the call is latency-critical on a hot path: an indirection through a registry per call buys nothing.

Plugin code cannot be trusted and no isolation (subprocess, sandbox, capability gate) is available: expose the extension point as a service over a process or network boundary instead of loading third-party code in-process.
anti_patterns: A "plugin system" that is really a switch over a fixed set of built-in implementations selected by configuration; nothing can be added without editing and rebuilding the host.
A contract that changes with every host release - the open/closed principle wearing an interface, which puts every plugin author on the host's release train.
Loading third-party code in-process with full host privileges and no capability gate, version check or shared compliance suite.
Plugins reaching into host internals (globals, private members, filesystem layout) instead of the published framework interface, so any internal refactoring breaks the ecosystem.
Registration-order dependence: the host invokes extension points before plugins have registered, so behaviour silently varies with start-up timing.
Reloading plugins without draining references and registrations, leaving threads, handles and cache entries behind on every cycle.
Trusting plugin manifest claims without validating capabilities at load time; a malicious or buggy plugin declares more than it delivers.
Loading all plugins eagerly at startup instead of lazy-activating on first use, bloating startup time and memory for features the session never exercises.
design_principles: Dependency inversion: host and plugin both depend on the published contract, never on each other's concrete code.
Open/closed principle: the host is closed to modification and open to extension through its declared extension points.
Separation of concerns: the core owns policy, discovery and lifecycle; plugins own the volatile capability.
Stable dependencies: the contract must be more stable than the host internals - keep it narrow, documented and versioned.
Least privilege: publish only the host services a plugin needs, and isolate code that is not fully trusted.
Fail-closed: reject plugins whose contract version or declared capabilities do not match, rather than degrading silently.
best_practices: Declare extension points explicitly, document their semantics, and treat the contract as a public API with its own version and compatibility test suite.
Discover before you load: read descriptors or metadata (id, version, required contract, capabilities) without executing plugin code, so one broken plugin cannot break discovery.
Validate at the boundary and fail closed: check contract/ABI version and required capabilities at load time and refuse a mismatching plugin instead of degrading silently.
Give every plugin a lifecycle (load, activate, deactivate, unload) driven from one registry; activate only after all registrations, unload in reverse dependency order.
Isolate to the level of trust: separate class loaders or load contexts for dependency conflicts, a subprocess or sandbox for third-party code, in-process only for code you own.
Keep per-plugin observability - metrics, timeouts and failure containment - so one plugin cannot stall the host pipeline unnoticed.
Test unload, not only load: run repeated load/unload cycles and watch memory, handle and thread counts for leaks.

Use lazy activation events: load plugins only when their extension point is first needed, not at startup, to keep memory and startup time proportional to actual use (see VS Code extension host, Grafana plugin lifecycle).

Version contracts additively: add new optional members or callbacks at the end of the ABI struct; keep existing offsets frozen so older plugins keep working on newer hosts (see Terraform plugin protocol, OS-level ABI stability patterns).

Declare capability manifests allowlist-only: plugins should only access what they declare, with host-mediated callbacks for privileged operations (HTTP, secrets, network) rather than direct access (see Flux capability sandbox, WordPress EmDash sandbox).
Implement graceful degradation: if a plugin fails to load or activate, log a clear error and continue with the remaining plugins rather than crashing the host.
Document the dependency order explicitly: plugins that depend on other plugins should declare it, and the registry should topologically sort activation order.
sources: Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002) - Plugin, by David Rice and Matt Foemmel (Distribution Strategies); the pattern links classes during configuration rather than compilation through a plugin factory that maps types to implementations (ch. 18).
Marquardt, Patterns for Plug-Ins, EuroPLoP 1999, and Pattern Languages of Program Design Vol. 5 - host application, plug-in contract, plug-in registration and plug-in lifecycle.

Pluggable Systems as Architectural Pattern, Proceedings of the 2015 European Conference on Software Architecture Workshops - treats pluggable systems as a higher-level pattern enabling ecosystem-scale properties with Eclipse as case study.

Plug-in Architecture and Design Guidelines for Customizable Enterprise Applications, OOPSLA 2008 - lightweight core with slot-and-extension mechanism, dynamic reconfiguration, plug-in isolation and security controls.
Painless Plugins, Imperial College London - investigates plugin architectures for dynamic construction, modular upgrades and reduced configuration burden.
Modelling a Framework for Plugins, Imperial College London - general flexible plugin architecture extending applications at runtime through plugin component composition via interfaces.
Architectural Consistency Checking in Plugin-Based Software Systems, RWTH Aachen - DepCoL domain-specific language for enforcing constraints on plugin and feature dependencies.
On Plug-ins and Extensible Architectures, ACM Queue - examines pure plug-in architectures as a universal software design pattern and how hosting environments evolve.

VS Code Extension Host Architecture - multi-process isolation model with separate extension host (Node.js/WebWorker), lazy activation events, and contribution points for declarative extension registration.
Terraform Plugin Protocol (gRPC-based), HashiCorp - standalone executable plugins communicating via protobuf APIs with major version handshake negotiation for backward/forward compatibility.

Hardhat Plugin Lifecycle - two-phase lifecycle (import and HRE initialization), lazy-loaded actions via setAction(), explicit hook registration/unregistration, and ordered plugin dependency resolution.
Grafana Plugin Lifecycle - discovery, validation, and runtime loading phases differing by plugin type (panel, datasource, app) with backend presence considerations.
Kibana Plugin Performance Guide - lazy-loading UI components in mount handlers, bundle splitting strategies, and @kbn/optimizer profiling for perceived performance.
Microkernel Pattern, Metapatterns - thin core as middleware connecting external services with internal resource providers via SPIs; specialisation of the plugin pattern with layered orchestration.
Flux Plugin Capability Sandbox - allow-by-manifest capability model with host-mediated callbacks, deny-by-default posture, and OS process sandbox for defence-in-depth.
Platypus Plugin API Versioning - additive contract evolution within major versions; major version bumps for required member changes; core supports N and N-1 during transitions.
OSaurus Plugin ABI Versioning - append-only ABI evolution with frozen field offsets, forward/backward compatibility via defensive version checks, and RESERVED slots for removed callbacks.
Silo Plugin SDK Compatibility - semver-governed public build-time contract with additive protobuf evolution as the long-term compatibility source of truth.
WooCommerce Selective Plugin Loading - route-specific plugin allowlisting to exclude irrelevant plugins per request, achieving >50% memory reduction and significant latency improvements.
